The paixiao is an ancient Chinese blown aerophone, a panpipe form of the xiao family. It is built from bamboo pipes of different lengths set in order and bound with bamboo strips; the top of each pipe is cut at a slant or notched, so that the pitch can be bent down a semitone as on the dongxiao, which lets semitones be played without spoiling the tone. The player holds the top of the frame with both hands, the mouthpiece facing forward, the lower lip against the mouthpiece, and blows pipe by pipe according to the pitch. It was once an important instrument of high antiquity alongside the bianzhong and bianqing chimes, circulated among the people from the Spring and Autumn period to the Qin and Han, took a larger role in Han music, and from the Northern and Southern Dynasties to the Sui and Tang became an important instrument of court yayue, spreading to Goguryeo, Kucha and Japan; the Korean so developed from it and is used in ancestral rites.
排簫為中國氣鳴樂器。其曾與編鐘、編磬同為上古重要樂器，春秋至秦漢在民間流傳，漢代: The paixiao is a Chinese aerophone. It was once an important instrument of high antiquity alongside the bianzhong and bianqing chimes, circulated among the people from the Spring and Autumn period to the Qin and Han, and took a larger role in Han music; from the Northern and Southern Dynasties to the Sui and Tang it became court yayue and spread to Goguryeo, Kucha and Japan. The Korean so evolved from the paixiao and is used in ancestral rites. In modern times the Jilin Opera developed a double-row paixiao that can play both lyrical and lively music; in the Tang music-and-dance programme at the Shaanxi Grand Theatre in Xi'an, the paidi is played.
排簫為氣鳴樂器，演奏時以雙手握住簫架頂端，吹口朝前，下唇貼於吹口，依音高尋找對應: The paixiao is an aerophone: the player holds the top of the frame with both hands, the mouthpiece facing forward, the lower lip against the mouthpiece, and blows into the pipe that matches each pitch. A beginner can start by learning which pipe gives which pitch and playing them one at a time. On the Chinese paixiao the tops of the pipes are cut at a slant or notched, so the pitch can be bent while playing.
排簫發聲體以竹管為主，戰國曾侯乙墓出土者用十三根長短不同的竹管排成，並以三根竹管: The sounding body of the paixiao is mainly bamboo pipes: the example from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng has thirteen pipes of different lengths bound with three bamboo strips, and the Korean so has sixteen bamboo pipes. There is also a Western Zhou panpipe of bone, showing that bone was used early on. The Qianlong paixiao of the Qing has sixteen pipes with note names carved on them and gold cloud-dragon ornament on the frame, but the materials of the frame and the ornament are not stated. The source also says nothing about the materials of the other parts of modern improved paixiao and of the side-blown types.
排簫音色溫潤而富有詩意，具有柔和、內斂的質感，既不過於明亮刺耳，亦不顯得沉悶晦暗: The paixiao's timbre is warm and poetic, soft and inward, neither too bright and harsh nor dull and dark. Its range is wide, from low to high, with many layers. Because the pipes sound side by side, the tone has a particular thickness and depth: the pipes answer one another and produce a sound that turns back on itself and lingers. Compared with a single recorder, the paixiao is fuller and more embracing; compared with the bianzhong chimes, its tone is more flowing and smoother. Its character is archaic and refined, and it tends to give an impression of stillness and distance, of something lifted out of the world; in ancient ensembles it played a lyrical role of its own.
